name: English (Received Pronunciation)
variety: Received Pronunciation in its mainstream form (also called General British or Standard Southern British English), with conservative and recent variants noted
sources: Roach, Peter (2004). British English: Received Pronunciation. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 34(2), 239-245.
Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. 3 volumes. Cambridge University Press.
Cruttenden, Alan (2014). Gimson's Pronunciation of English. 8th edition. London: Routledge.
Deterding, David (1997). The formants of monophthong vowels in Standard Southern British English pronunciation. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 27, 47-55.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Docherty, Gerard J. (1992). The Timing of Voicing in British English Obstruents. Berlin: Foris.
O'Connor, J. D. and Arnold, G. F. (1973). Intonation of Colloquial English. 2nd edition. London: Longman.
Cruttenden, Alan (1997). Intonation. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Wells, J. C. (2006). English Intonation: An Introduction. Cambridge University Press.
Lindsey, Geoff (2019). English After RP: Standard British Pronunciation Today. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.

vowel_formants.speaker: mean of five adult male BBC broadcasters, vowels measured in connected speech

contrasts: FOOT versus STRUT: /ʊ/ and /ʌ/ are separate phonemes (put versus putt)
TRAP versus BATH: BATH words have the long back vowel of PALM and START, /ɑː/ (ant versus aunt, gas versus grass)
non-rhotic: historical /r/ after a vowel is lost, which gives the long vowels /ɑː ɔː ɜː/ and the centring diphthongs /ɪə eə ʊə/ (card, cord, bird, near, square, cure)
LOT versus THOUGHT (cot versus caught) and PALM versus LOT (balm versus bomb)
long versus short monophthongs, which differ in quality as well as length (beat versus bit, pool versus pull)
voiced versus voiceless obstruents in all positions, cued at the end of a word mainly by the length of the vowel before them
dental fricatives /θ ð/ versus /f v/ and /t d/
lexical stress (import as noun versus verb), with reduction of unstressed vowels
allophony: /p t k/ are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable, unaspirated after /s/, and weakly released or glottally reinforced at the end of a syllable
/t/ is often a glottal stop before a consonant and, for younger speakers, before a pause (not now, that one); between vowels it stays [t]
vowels are clipped before voiceless consonants: the long vowel of beat is about as short as the short vowel of bid
/b d ɡ dʒ v ð z ʒ/ are only partly voiced next to a pause or a voiceless sound
/l/ is clear before vowels and /j/, dark [ɫ] before consonants and pause; dark /l/ may be vocalised in recent speech

/ɹ/ is a postalveolar approximant and occurs only before vowels; a linking /r/ appears when a word-final non-high vowel is followed by a vowel (far away), and an intrusive /r/ in the same position where the spelling has none (law and order, idea of)
final unstressed happY is [i] for most present-day speakers and [ɪ] for conservative ones
/uː/ is fronted to [ʉː], and /ʊ/ is centralised and unrounded for many speakers
/æ/ has lowered towards [a] in recent decades
/ʊə/ is giving way to /ɔː/ (poor, sure), less often after /j/ (cure, pure); /eə/ is commonly a long monophthong [ɛː]; /ɪə/ is tending to [ɪː]
/aɪə aʊə/ are smoothed to [aə ɑə] or to long monophthongs in fast speech (fire, power)
/tj dj/ coalesce to [tʃ dʒ] in unstressed syllables and increasingly in stressed ones (tune, due)
syllabic [n̩ l̩] replace schwa plus sonorant after most consonants (button, bottle)
function words have weak forms with schwa (and, of, to, was, can)
phonotactics: the short vowels /ɪ e æ ɒ ʌ ʊ/ need a following consonant in a stressed syllable
/ŋ/ does not begin a syllable and follows only short vowels; /h/ only begins a syllable; /ʒ/ is rare at the edges of words
onsets of three consonants begin with /s/ followed by a voiceless stop and an approximant (spl, spr, str, skr, skw)
codas have up to four consonants (texts, sixths)

stress.rule: Stress is fixed for each word and not predictable from one rule: Germanic words stress the first syllable of the root, Latinate words mostly stress a heavy penultimate syllable and otherwise the antepenultimate, and many suffixes fix the stress of the word.
stress.cues: pitch movement on accented syllables, duration, loudness and vowel quality (full vowels against schwa, [ɪ] and syllabic consonants)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: most unstressed syllables have schwa, [ɪ], [i], [u] or a syllabic consonant
rhythm.notes: The nPVI value comes from one speaker of Southern British English reading a text.

length.notes: Five long monophthongs contrast with seven short ones, always with a difference of quality. The length of a vowel depends strongly on the following consonant (pre-fortis clipping). Long consonants occur only across morpheme and word boundaries (unknown, this side).

intonation.declarative: a high head that steps down through the accented syllables, and a falling nuclear tone (high fall or low fall) on the last accented word, ending low
intonation.yes_no_question: low rise or high rise on the nucleus; a fall is also common
intonation.wh_question: falling nuclear tone; a rise makes the question sound kind or tentative
intonation.continuation: fall-rise or low rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: nuclear fall (H* L): the pitch is high on the accented syllable and falls within it or over the following syllables; prenuclear accents are high level steps
intonation.notes: Nuclear tones in the British tradition: high fall, low fall, low rise, high rise, fall-rise, rise-fall and mid level.

phonation: glottal reinforcement of syllable-final /p t k tʃ/ and glottal replacement of /t/
creaky voice on low pitch at the end of falling utterances is common

problems: final unstressed happY is lax [ɪ] (the voice replaces the final vowel by the phoneme i, which has KIT quality in this table): this is the conservative form, while most present-day speakers have [i]
all CURE words have [ɔː] (cure [kjɔː], poor [pɔː]); many speakers keep [ʊə] after /j/
there is no glottal reinforcement or glottal replacement of /t/
wh-questions get the same rising tune as yes-no questions, because the tune is chosen from the question mark alone; statements, commas and exclamations use the default English tunes
NEAR and SQUARE are the older centring diphthongs; the monophthongal [ɛː] of present-day speech is not available
good: TRAP is [æ] and BATH has the long back [ɑː] of PALM, so the TRAP-BATH split is complete
non-rhotic, with linking and intrusive r before a following vowel
clear and dark /l/ by position, aspirated stops, shorter vowels before voiceless consonants
GOOSE is fronted and GOAT starts with a central vowel [əʊ]
word-final schwa is an open [ɐ] (letter, comma), as in RP before a pause

notes: In the vowel list [i] is the unstressed vowel of happY. I give no voice onset time values: Docherty (1992) is the source to consult, and I cannot quote his figures with confidence.
